paragraphs: Predicting how objects move from images can look like learning physical rules, but strong performance in familiar environments does not establish that those rules transfer elsewhere. This paper investigates that gap using RPCIN, a model for long-term dynamics prediction that takes images and basic object descriptions, including bounding boxes and segmentation masks.

The authors introduce four datasets: SimB-Border, SimB-Split, BlenB-Border, and BlenB-Split. Together, these cover two domains and two contexts, allowing experiments on both Cross-Domain and Cross-Context environment misalignment. Testing RPCIN across combinations of these datasets makes changes in the environment a central part of evaluation rather than treating prediction accuracy in one setting as sufficient evidence of broader capability.

The experiments reveal potential weaknesses in RPCIN under these changes. The paper also presents a direction for addressing the Cross-Domain challenge and reports substantial improvement on its proposed datasets. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and constructive: it supplies targeted tests of transfer and evidence for a possible remedy, while grounding its findings in the model and environments actually examined.
icml-2023-a-critical-view-of-vision-base.tldr: New datasets expose environment-transfer weaknesses in vision-based dynamics prediction and support a promising way to reduce the Cross-Domain problem.

paragraphs: Attention-based vision models can perform well while requiring substantial storage and computation. This paper studies compression through model factorization, an approach that had received less attention for vision transformers than pruning. Its aim is to expand the available ways of producing compact models while preserving useful predictive performance.

COMCAT develops a compression method from an insight into multi-head attention. The reported ImageNet comparisons show that compressed DeiT-small and DeiT-base models achieve higher top-1 accuracy than state-of-the-art pruning methods, with reported gains of 0.45% and 0.76%, respectively, despite using fewer parameters. These results indicate that the structure of attention offers compression opportunities beyond simply removing parts of a model.

The authors also apply their finding to customization of text-to-image diffusion models. They report training speedups of up to 2.6 times and reductions in extra storage of up to 1927.5 times relative to existing approaches. These are reported maxima for the evaluated settings. Together, the applications connect attention compression with the practical cost of both deploying vision models and maintaining customized generative models.
icml-2023-comcat-towards-efficient-compr.tldr: COMCAT uses attention-based factorization to compress vision transformers and reduce the training and storage costs of diffusion-model customization.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links an upper-level objective to a lower-level optimization problem. In federated learning, computing the upper-level gradient, called a hypergradient, is particularly challenging because the required curvature information is distributed across participants. The paper identifies the nonlinear construction of sequences of global Hessian matrices as a major obstacle to efficient communication.

The proposed estimator, aggregated iterative differentiation or AggITD, computes hypergradient information while lower-level optimization is taking place. Performing these operations together substantially reduces communication. The authors show that an algorithm using AggITD attains the same sample complexity as existing approaches based on approximate implicit differentiation, while requiring far fewer communication rounds even when participants have heterogeneous data.

This result separates the cost of using data from the cost of exchanging information. It also changes the comparison between differentiation strategies: iterative differentiation has an advantage here despite being less efficient than approximate implicit differentiation in the non-distributed comparison discussed by the authors. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness and communication efficiency, reinforcing the importance of designing optimization procedures around the distributed setting.
icml-2023-communication-efficient-federa.tldr: AggITD combines lower-level optimization with hypergradient estimation to reduce federated communication without worsening the stated sample complexity.

paragraphs: Ad hoc teamwork asks an agent to cooperate with unfamiliar teammates without arranging a strategy beforehand. A common approach groups teammates into broad types and trains a response for each type. This paper shows why that abstraction can be misleading when training ignores how individual teammates are distributed within each group.

The problem, called type confounding, can be severe: in the worst case, the response judged best for a type can be worst for every individual assigned to it. Through causal analysis, the authors attribute this phenomenon to spurious correlations introduced by an uncontrolled distribution of teammate instances. The apparent value of a response can therefore reflect which teammates produced the feedback rather than reliable guidance for cooperation.

Their method, CTCAT, adjusts feedback at the level of individual teammate instances. It reweights interactions within a shared type to reduce the influence of the confounding correlation. Evaluations across classic teamwork tasks and real-world scenarios show robustness to type confounding. The findings make the composition of teammate groups an explicit concern when training agents to cooperate with new partners.
icml-2023-controlling-type-confounding-i.tldr: CTCAT reweights feedback from individual teammates to reduce misleading correlations hidden inside broad teammate types.

paragraphs: GAN-based super-resolution can reconstruct realistic-looking detail while also producing unwanted visual artifacts. The paper focuses on artifacts that appear in previously unseen real images, where ground-truth high-resolution versions are unavailable. It argues that training-time artifact penalties remain tied to the artifact types encountered during training, leaving problems when models are used in practice.

DeSRA first detects suspicious regions by comparing outputs from an MSE-based super-resolution model and a GAN-based model. Its signal is a relative distance between their local variances, combined with thresholds that account for semantic content. This comparison provides a way to locate problematic areas without requiring a correct reference image for the new input.

After detection, DeSRA uses a few samples in a fine-tuning procedure that improves the GAN-based model’s handling of similar artifacts in further unseen data. The authors report successful artifact removal and improved practical applicability. The central contribution is a correction process informed by failures observed during actual use, connecting artifact localization with model adaptation rather than relying entirely on the original training penalty.
icml-2023-desra-detect-and-delete-the-ar.tldr: DeSRA detects super-resolution artifacts without ground-truth images and uses a few examples to fine-tune the model against similar failures.

paragraphs: This paper studies private reinforcement learning when rewards may have heavy tails, allowing unusually large observations beyond the bounded or sub-Gaussian reward assumptions common in earlier work. The setting is a finite-horizon tabular Markov decision process. Its reward assumption requires only a finite moment of order 1+v, where v lies between zero and one inclusive.

The authors use robust reward-mean estimators to develop two frameworks, one based on value iteration and one on policy optimization. Each framework accommodates both joint differential privacy and local differential privacy. Their regret upper bounds describe how learning performance depends on the available privacy budget and the reward distribution’s moment condition.

The paper also establishes regret lower bounds for both privacy models. For joint privacy, the argument reduces the problem to private heavy-tailed multi-armed bandits; for local privacy, it uses private minimax methods. These bounds address fundamental obstacles as well as algorithm performance. The results show that heavy-tailed rewards change the private learning problem in substantive ways, making reward-tail assumptions central to understanding the attainable privacy–performance tradeoff.
icml-2023-differentially-private-episodi.tldr: Robust reward estimation enables private reinforcement learning under heavy tails, with regret bounds exposing the roles of privacy and reward moments.

paragraphs: A classifier can succeed for the wrong reason, such as recognizing cats through their frequent association with beds. That shortcut becomes unreliable when the background changes. This paper addresses such spurious correlations while also seeking to make the correction process understandable, so that improvements come with insight into what the model was relying on.

Discover and Cure, or DISC, works iteratively with concepts that people can interpret. It first identifies concepts whose behavior is unstable across environments and treats them as spurious attributes. It then uses those discoveries to intervene on the training data and reduce the unwanted association. Repeating discovery and intervention connects diagnosis directly to changes in learning.

The authors report better generalization and interpretability than existing approaches across their experiments. They state improvements of 7.5% on an object recognition task and 9.6% on a skin-lesion classification task over state-of-the-art methods. The paper also supplies theoretical analysis and guarantees for benefits of DISC-trained models. Its contribution combines a practical mitigation procedure with an interpretable account of the concepts being targeted.
icml-2023-discover-and-cure-concept-awar.tldr: DISC identifies unstable, interpretable concepts and changes training data to reduce the spurious correlations they reveal.

paragraphs: Evaluating a policy from existing data becomes harder when that data was collected using a different policy. This paper estimates the full distribution of the target policy’s return, rather than only a single average. It also allows rewards to have several components, making the object of prediction a potentially complicated joint distribution.

The proposed Fitted Likelihood Estimation algorithm repeatedly solves maximum-likelihood learning problems. This design can incorporate probabilistic generative models provided they can be trained through maximum likelihood. The framework covers both finite-horizon problems and infinite-horizon problems with discounted rewards, giving the same broad estimation strategy a role in two different decision-making settings.

The guarantees depend on offline data covering the target policy’s trajectories and on successful maximum-likelihood learning. Under those conditions, the estimated distributions approach the truth in total variation distance for the finite-horizon case and Wasserstein distance for the discounted infinite-horizon case. Experiments use Gaussian mixture and diffusion models. In particular, the diffusion-based version demonstrates the ability to estimate complicated return distributions when rewards are multidimensional.
icml-2023-distributional-offline-policy-.tldr: Fitted Likelihood Estimation learns policy-return distributions from offline data, with error guarantees conditional on coverage and successful likelihood training.

paragraphs: Image matting estimates an object’s opacity mask so it can be separated from its surroundings. Because the image alone leaves substantial ambiguity, existing methods often ask users to supply trimaps or scribbles. Producing those inputs can take time and may require knowing which parts of the image most need guidance.

dugMatting divides uncertainty into two components and addresses them differently. It reduces epistemic uncertainty through guided interaction that introduces prior knowledge. It addresses aleatoric uncertainty by modeling the data distribution, including statistics associated with possible noise. This explicit separation gives the framework distinct ways to use human input and statistical modeling when improving the opacity estimate.

The interaction framework reduces the burden on users to decide where they should provide information, instead supporting simple labeling guided by the method. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report significant gains in efficiency and effectiveness over the original matting algorithms. The practical contribution is a more directed interaction process: uncertainty helps determine how additional information should enter the system, making user effort more useful to the matting result.
icml-2023-dugmatting-decomposed-uncertai.tldr: dugMatting separates uncertainty sources to guide user input and statistical modeling, improving image matting efficiency and quality.

paragraphs: Fairness requirements can change the best classification accuracy a model can achieve. This paper characterizes that tradeoff for demographic parity in settings with multiple demographic groups, multiple classes, and noise. Its analysis concerns classifiers that may randomize their decisions and use demographic attributes, making those features part of the stated optimization setting.

The authors show that the lowest achievable classification error under the fairness requirement equals the solution of a Wasserstein-barycenter problem. This mathematical characterization turns the fairness–accuracy tradeoff into an explicit optimization target. It describes the best attainable error within the specified classifier class, rather than merely comparing a collection of particular training procedures.

The theory leads to a simple post-processing method that converts score functions into fair classifiers. When the supplied scores are Bayes optimal, the resulting fair classifier is optimal as well. The paper also analyzes suboptimality and sample complexity and evaluates the method on benchmark datasets. Its practical significance is that fairness can be imposed through a principled transformation of scores, with the strongest optimality conclusion explicitly tied to the quality of those scores.
icml-2023-fair-and-optimal-classificatio.tldr: The paper characterizes the demographic-parity accuracy tradeoff and derives post-processing that is optimal when its input scores are Bayes optimal.

paragraphs: Learning even a single ReLU neuron raises meaningful questions when input dimension exceeds the number of examples. This paper studies that setting under squared loss, analyzing the Perceptron-type algorithm GLM-tron. The goal is to characterize prediction risk with a finite amount of data rather than relying only on eventual convergence.

The authors establish dimension-free risk upper bounds in both well-specified and misspecified settings. When the model is well-specified, they also give a matching lower bound for each problem instance. Together, these results sharply describe which high-dimensional ReLU regression problems GLM-tron can learn, while recovering several earlier results as special cases.

The comparison with stochastic gradient descent is made for symmetric Bernoulli data. In the well-specified setting, SGD’s excess risk is no better than GLM-tron’s up to constant factors on each instance. In the noiseless case, GLM-tron can obtain small risk while SGD retains constant expected risk. These findings support GLM-tron as a potentially preferable choice for this problem class; the stated data and model conditions are essential to interpreting the comparison.
icml-2023-finite-sample-analysis-of-lear.tldr: Sharp risk bounds for GLM-tron and conditional negative results for SGD favor GLM-tron in the studied high-dimensional ReLU regression settings.

paragraphs: Return-conditioned learning trains decision models using desired rewards, but this requires reward labels in the training data. This paper develops a way to pretrain from offline trajectories that lack those labels and may contain suboptimal behavior. Its Pretrained Decision Transformer, or PDT, replaces reward-specific conditioning during pretraining with information about future trajectories.

During training, the model uses future trajectory information as privileged context for predicting actions. This allows it to learn relationships between present situations, actions, and possible futures without initially requiring a numerical return for each behavior. For online fine-tuning, the method can assign returns to possible futures and sample their embeddings according to those values, connecting unsupervised pretraining to return-conditioned decision making.

Experiments show that PDT matches or exceeds its supervised-pretraining counterpart, particularly with suboptimal data. Further analysis indicates that the model extracts diverse behaviors from offline trajectories and can be fine-tuned to controllably select high-return behavior. The contribution is a route from reward-free behavioral data to value-guided decisions, with future information serving as the link between those learning stages.
icml-2023-future-conditioned-unsupervise.tldr: PDT learns from reward-free trajectories by conditioning on future behavior, then uses online fine-tuning to favor high-return futures.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether effective human study techniques can inspire better machine-learning training procedures. Its focus is bilevel optimization, where learning involves two linked optimization levels. Rather than treating a classroom analogy as a complete algorithm, the authors build a framework for expressing different learning arrangements through configurable components.

The framework, Skillearn, includes learners, interaction functions, and learning stages. These elements can be combined to create strategies that emulate particular study techniques. The authors develop case studies inspired by the Feynman technique and peer questioning, using them to construct new training strategies. The framework’s flexibility is central: different interactions and stages can represent different ways of organizing learning.

The resulting strategies are applied to neural architecture search and data weighting, two applications based on bilevel optimization. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate their effectiveness in those applications. The contribution is both a general vocabulary for designing training interactions and concrete examples showing that this design approach can improve learning outcomes. The reported evidence concerns the implemented strategies and applications, rather than establishing that every human study technique will transfer successfully.
icml-2023-improving-bi-level-optimizatio.tldr: Skillearn turns human study techniques into configurable training strategies that improve the tested bilevel optimization applications.

paragraphs: The learning target in this paper is a function that assigns a probability distribution over labels to each feature input. Labels are sampled independently from these feature-dependent distributions, then passed through a noisy mechanism in privacy-sensitive applications. The learner therefore tries to recover the underlying label probabilities using observations whose labels have been altered.

The setting is online: at each step, predictions use the available features and noisy labels from earlier steps. Performance is measured by expected KL-risk, which compares predicted distributions with the true ones. For a finite hypothesis class F and any non-trivial noise level, the authors establish a minimax rate of order square root of T times log of the size of F, up to logarithmic factors.

The paper then extends the analysis to infinite hypothesis classes using stochastic sequential covering. Matching upper and lower bounds are obtained for a broad range of natural classes. These paired bounds describe both achievable learning performance and unavoidable difficulty, connecting noisy-label distribution prediction to the complexity of the class of possible functions.
icml-2023-learning-functional-distributi.tldr: The paper establishes matching learning-risk bounds for online prediction of label distributions from privacy-noised labels.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe learned systems through continuous dynamics. This paper addresses how to make those dynamics satisfy specified output requirements. Its central idea is invariance set propagation: using mathematical constraints to keep the evolving system within the behavior permitted by its output specifications.

The method uses a class of control barrier functions to translate output requirements into constraints on the learning system’s parameters and inputs. Adjusting those constrained quantities allows the method to enforce output guarantees during both training and inference. This makes the requirements actionable through variables the system can change, connecting a desired property of the output to the internal choices that govern its evolution.

For data-controlled neural ODEs, the authors demonstrate that this approach maintains generalization performance while adding robustness through causal manipulation of parameters and inputs. Tests include representation learning for physical dynamics and convexity portraits, alongside collision avoidance for autonomous vehicles. The work links learned continuous dynamics with explicit specification enforcement, showing how interventions on model parameters or inputs can support both prediction and controlled behavior.
icml-2023-on-the-forward-invariance-of-n.tldr: Invariance set propagation converts neural ODE output requirements into parameter and input constraints enforceable during training and inference.

paragraphs: The order in which SGD encounters examples can interact strongly with batch normalization. This paper compares Single Shuffle, which uses a single shuffled ordering, with Random Reshuffle, which refreshes the ordering. It finds that Random Reshuffle produces substantially more stable training-loss evolution, showing that these two common variants can behave quite differently.

For regression with a linear network and batch-normalized inputs, the authors prove that the two methods converge to distinct global optima displaced from the gradient-descent solution. For classification, they characterize conditions under which either method can or cannot diverge. These analyses distinguish changes in the solution reached from failures of training to remain stable.

The paper also gives explicit constructions in which Single Shuffle produces distorted regression optima or classification divergence while Random Reshuffle avoids those problems. This does not turn the broader analysis into an unconditional guarantee for reshuffling. Empirical tests in realistic settings support the practical relevance of the separation. The findings make the shuffling procedure part of understanding optimization behavior when batch normalization is present.
icml-2023-on-the-training-instability-of.tldr: Batch normalization can make Single Shuffle and Random Reshuffle behave differently, with reshuffling showing greater stability in the studied settings.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning aims to fit models to individual clients while retaining the privacy-oriented benefits of federated training. This paper argues that focusing mainly on differences in the relationship between inputs and labels can overlook another source of heterogeneity: clients may also receive different kinds of inputs. That input-distribution shift can undermine personalization.

FedGMM addresses this issue by using Gaussian mixture models to fit input distributions across clients. Its parameters are estimated through maximum likelihood with a federated expectation-maximization algorithm that has a closed-form solution. The method does not assume that clients have similar gradients, which matters because the approach explicitly accommodates differences in their data.

The resulting model also supports uncertainty quantification and adaptation to new clients with minimal overhead. Experiments on synthetic data and benchmark datasets report superior performance for personalized classification and detection of novel samples. These two evaluation tasks reflect the method’s dual purpose: fitting client-specific predictions while modeling what kinds of inputs clients encounter. The contribution places input-distribution modeling at the center of personalization and adaptation.
icml-2023-personalized-federated-learnin.tldr: FedGMM models differing client input distributions to improve personalized federated classification, novel-sample detection, and adaptation to new clients.

paragraphs: Foundation models can handle many tasks, yet transfer learning may leave useful relationships between those tasks unexplored. Predict-Interpolate Tuning, or π-Tuning, uses lightweight experts learned for related tasks to help a target task. It applies to vision, language, and combined vision-language problems while keeping adaptation parameter-efficient.

The method first predicts task similarity in a shared space that does not depend on modality. It then combines parameters from relevant task-specific experts. This prediction-then-interpolation procedure can use different expert forms, including prompts and adapters. Its task graph also exposes relationships between tasks, supporting interpretation of which transfers are useful within a modality and across modalities.

The authors study 14 unimodal and six multimodal datasets, reporting that π-Tuning exceeds full fine-tuning and other parameter-efficient transfer methods in both full-shot and low-shot settings. They also report improvements in transfer accuracy and robustness, especially when data is scarce. The approach makes existing task adaptations reusable resources: the target task benefits from selecting and combining relevant expertise, with the task graph helping explain those choices.
icml-2023-pi-tuning-transferring-multimo.tldr: π-Tuning predicts task relationships and combines lightweight experts to improve transfer across vision, language, and multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Variational quantum algorithms depend on the design of parameterized quantum circuits. This paper studies how to automate that design through quantum architecture search. The authors aim to reduce reliance on approaches that require sampling and evaluating many candidate circuits, proposing a differentiable search algorithm based on Gumbel-Softmax.

QuantumDARTS offers two search modes. Macro search directly searches for the structure of an entire circuit. Micro search instead learns a sub-circuit structure on a smaller problem and transfers it to a larger one. That distinction gives the method two ways to organize architecture discovery: whole-circuit design and reuse of structures identified at a smaller scale.

Experiments cover unweighted Max-Cut, ground-state energy estimation, and image classification. The reported performance supports the efficiency and capability of macro search while requiring little prior knowledge. The micro-search experiments suggest potential for larger-scale quantum architecture search, rather than establishing a universal scaling result. Together, the two modes explore how differentiable architecture selection and transferable circuit components can support the automatic design of variational quantum algorithms.
icml-2023-quantumdarts-differentiable-qu.tldr: QuantumDARTS uses differentiable search to design whole quantum circuits or transfer sub-circuit structures learned on smaller problems.

paragraphs: Image restoration benefits from relationships between distant parts of an image, but attending across large images can be costly. Local-window transformers keep computation manageable by restricting attention to small regions. This paper asks how those efficient local computations can also capture information from locations that were originally far apart.

The proposed strategy randomly shuffles the input before applying local self-attention. Shuffling can place originally distant elements within the same local attention group. The authors ground this idea in the permutation-equivariance of self-attention and provide theoretical guarantees for extending its local scope. The strategy introduces no additional parameters, so the broader interaction pattern does not require a larger learned parameter set.

The resulting model, ShuffleFormer, combines efficient processing of high-resolution images with the ability to model non-local interactions. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness on denoising, deraining, and deblurring. The contribution is a change in how input elements are grouped for attention: rearranging them allows local computations to reach beyond their original spatial neighborhoods while retaining the practical motivation for window-based processing.
icml-2023-random-shuffle-transformer-for.tldr: ShuffleFormer randomly rearranges inputs so efficient local attention can model distant image relationships without adding parameters.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy’s performance using data collected under a different policy. This paper studies how precisely that evaluation can be done when the environment is a linear Markov decision process with a known feature map. The known structure is central because it informs both the achievable precision and the estimator’s construction.

The authors characterize a variance lower bound for regular estimators in this setting and propose an estimator that attains it. This is the sense in which the method is semiparametrically efficient: it reaches the stated statistical precision limit. They also establish consistency and asymptotic normality under mild conditions, requiring the sole infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter to be estimated at a convergence rate of n to the power of minus one quarter.

The analysis leads to an asymptotically valid confidence interval, allowing uncertainty to accompany the policy-value estimate. Simulation studies validate the results. The contribution combines an efficiency benchmark, an estimator that reaches it, and an inference procedure, showing how known MDP structure can inform statistically precise policy evaluation.
icml-2023-semiparametrically-efficient-o.tldr: For linear MDPs with known features, the paper derives a variance limit and an efficient policy-value estimator with asymptotically valid confidence intervals.

paragraphs: Large language models require substantial memory and computation, making numerical compression attractive for inference. SmoothQuant targets 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations without additional training. The paper identifies an asymmetry behind the challenge: weights are relatively easy to quantize, whereas activation outliers make low-precision activations harder to handle accurately.

SmoothQuant applies an offline, mathematically equivalent transformation that moves quantization difficulty from activations into weights. By smoothing activation outliers before quantization, it enables integer 8-bit computation for both sides of the models’ matrix multiplications. The authors demonstrate this approach across model families including OPT, BLOOM, GLM, MT-NLG, and LLaMA.

The reported results include speedups of up to 1.56 times and memory reductions of two times, with negligible accuracy loss. The method also enables serving a 530-billion-parameter model within a single node. These results connect the numerical transformation to practical deployment costs. The key idea is to redistribute the difficulty of representing values before lowering precision, allowing the easier-to-quantize weights to absorb more of the challenge posed by activations.
icml-2023-smoothquant-accurate-and-effic.tldr: SmoothQuant shifts activation quantization difficulty into weights, enabling efficient 8-bit LLM inference with negligible reported accuracy loss.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the stability of SGD restricts the solutions it can sustain, creating an implicit form of regularization. The authors revisit connections between stability and Hessian-based measures of sharpness. A central result states that a global minimum that is linearly stable for SGD must have Hessian trace at most 2 divided by the learning rate.

Gradient descent has a corresponding stability constraint only on the Hessian’s largest eigenvalue. The distinction matters because a trace constraint restricts curvature across directions collectively. For two-layer ReLU networks and diagonal linear networks, the authors connect these sharpness measures to parameter norms, then use those relationships to prove generalization results for stable SGD minima.

Within the analyzed settings, gradient descent’s stability-induced regularization is too weak to ensure satisfactory generalization. This provides an explanation for SGD’s often better generalization. The learning rate controls the strength of the restriction: increasing it tightens the permitted Hessian trace. Numerical experiments support the theoretical account, linking learning-rate-dependent stability to the quality of the solutions that SGD can maintain.
icml-2023-the-implicit-regularization-of.tldr: SGD stability imposes curvature constraints that yield generalization guarantees for two studied network classes and strengthen with the learning rate.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks cause triggered inputs to be assigned attacker-chosen labels. Many detectors focus on attacks that funnel inputs into one target class. This paper addresses the more general X2X setting, where arbitrary source classes can each have their own target, making the suspicious pattern more complex than a single shared destination.

UMD detects these attacks without supervision by jointly inferring suspicious source–target pairs. It first defines a transferability statistic and uses clustering to select candidate pairs. It then aggregates the sizes of reverse-engineered triggers for those pairs and evaluates the aggregate with an unsupervised, robust anomaly detector. Considering pairs together is central to handling attacks with multiple targets.

Evaluations on CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and Imagenette report detection-accuracy improvements of 17%, 4%, and 8%, respectively, over state-of-the-art detectors, including supervised ones. The authors also report strong detection against several adaptive attacks. These findings support joint analysis of class relationships as a way to broaden unsupervised backdoor detection beyond the single-target patterns that earlier methods primarily addressed.
icml-2023-umd-unsupervised-model-detecti.tldr: UMD jointly analyzes suspicious source–target class pairs to detect general X2X backdoors without supervision.

paragraphs: A poisoned model can behave normally on ordinary inputs while responding abnormally to a backdoor trigger. That combination makes attacks difficult to recognize: the unwanted behavior can coexist with apparently intact predictions elsewhere. This paper proposes the adaptability hypothesis to explain when and why such selective changes can occur in learning models.

The hypothesis grows out of theoretical analysis of classical kernel-based learning. It proposes that, for an effective attack, incorporating a new dataset should have only a small effect on predictions for original points when those points are distant from the new data. The relevant idea is that a model can adapt to additional data while leaving sufficiently separated existing predictions largely undisturbed.

The authors test the hypothesis using benchmark image datasets and state-of-the-art backdoor attacks on deep neural networks. The experiments corroborate it, extending the evidence beyond the kernel models used for the theoretical investigation. The resulting account identifies a property connected to attack effectiveness and offers a basis for reasoning about future attacks and defenses, while retaining the status of a proposed, empirically supported hypothesis.
icml-2023-understanding-backdoor-attacks.tldr: The adaptability hypothesis links backdoor effectiveness to learning new behavior while minimally disturbing predictions on distant original data.
